title: Xenophon's Memorabilia I: Socrates on piety, self-control, and virtue as practice
summary: Xenophon defends Socrates against the charges of impiety and corrupting the young, preserving his sayings and dialogues with Aristodemus, Antiphon, Critias and Charicles. Socrates argues that self-restraint is the foundation of virtue, that virtue must be constantly practiced, that being good beats seeming good, and that the gods care for humans.

principles.text: Self-restraint is the cornerstone of virtue and the base of the soul.
principles.quote: Does it not come to this, that every honest man is bound to look upon self-restraint as the very corner-stone of virtue: which he should seek to lay down as the basis and foundation of his soul?

principles.text: Needing little brings a person closest to the divine.
principles.quote: To have no wants at all is, to my mind, an attribute of Godhead; to have as few wants as possible the nearest approach to Godhead

principles.text: True joy comes from becoming better and gaining better friends, not from luxury.
principles.quote: But is the pleasured derived from all these put together half as joyous as the consciousness of becoming better oneself, of acquiring better and better friends?

principles.text: The best route to reputation is to actually be good at what you wish to be thought good at.
principles.quote: there was no better road to renown than the one by which a man became good at that wherein he desired to be reputed good.

principles.text: Wisdom should be shared with chosen friends, not sold to the first bidder.
principles.quote: he who sells it for money to the first bidder we name a sophist, as though one should say a man who prostitutes his wisdom

principles.text: Study human questions of justice, piety and courage rather than cosmic speculation.
principles.quote: What is piety? what is impiety? What is the beautiful? what the ugly? What the noble? what the base? What are meant by just and unjust?
